The U.S. Constitution is more than usually Delphic in describing the 
structure and the powers of the executive branch. Article 11 concerns itselt 
primarily with the election, compensation, and removal of the president 
and vice president. Other executive branch officials are mentioned in two 
contexts: (1) The president is empowered, with the advice a^ consent ot 
two-thirds of the Senate, to appoint and “commission” “officers ot the 
United States”; and (2) the president is authorized to demand “the opinion, 
in writing, of the principal officer in each of the executive departments 
upon any subject relating to the duties of their respective offices. The chie 
domestic power of the president is stated as a responsibility—“he shall take 
care that the laws be faithfully executed”—and is listed following 
assignments that the president make reports and recommendations to the 
Congress and “receive Ambassadors and other Public Ministers.
Perhaps even more surprising is that deeply contested debates 
regarding the nature and operation of the constitutional presidency persist 
even as administrative governance and power have grown steadily over 
more than two hundred years. This chapter highlights three of them. How 
is Article II most soundly read, through the lens of constitutional 
originahsm or in a more adaptive mode? And if originalism is the method 
of choice, how did the founding generation understand the Constitution s 
late 18th century prose? For example, who among those employed by the 
United States is an “officer,” either principal or “inferior?” How are 
“officers” who are not subject to impeachment to be removed? What is a 
“department?” How are “departments” to be created, staffed, and managed? 
What techniques are available to the president, beyond demanding reports 
in writing, to “execute” the laws? And finally, what institutional design of 
the executive branch best serves the nation’s contemporary needs? Are the 
president’s reins over the administrative establishment best held tightly or 
with some slack? The Roberts Court has tried to settle critical aspects of at 
least the first two of these debates—often in ways seemingly in tension 
with the jurisprudence of earlier decades—^but the Court’s often closely- 
divided opinions have hardly cooled the underlying controversies either 
within or beyond the halls of government.
